citation: Aruna Ranganathan and Xingqi Maggie Ye (UC Berkeley Haas). 'AI Doesn't Reduce Work—It Intensifies It'. Harvard Business Review, 9 February 2026. https://hbr.org/2026/02/ai-doesnt-reduce-work-it-intensifies-it ; Haas newsroom interview with Ye, 18 February 2026: https://newsroom.haas.berkeley.edu/ai-promised-to-free-up-workers-time-uc-berkeley-haas-researchers-found-the-opposite/
source_tier: Practitioner article in a business magazine reporting initial findings of in-progress academic research (not peer-reviewed; no separate paper found)
access_status: HBR article body paywalled: only headline, summary, intro and author bios opened. Haas newsroom interview with Ye opened via WebFetch (fully read, summarised by fetch tool). Two short HBR blockquotes seen via Simon Willison's post (simonwillison.net/2026/Feb/9/ai-intensifies-work/). [uncertain] on anything in the HBR body beyond those.
sponsor_and_incentive: No funding disclosed in the Haas interview. Authors are academics; HBR article also promotes an 'AI practice' framing. Funding not found [uncertain].
exact_quotes: Haas interview (Ye): 'I was on site regularly, observing work in real time.' | 'I conducted more than 40 semi-structured interviews across functional groups.' | 'Employees worked at a faster pace, took on a broader scope of tasks' and 'extended work into more hours of the day, often without being asked to do so' (attributed to the in-progress research). | 'expectations can gradually reset, and what was once extra effort becomes standard performance.' | 'the workday becomes denser and more cognitively demanding.' | 'constant switching and reduced recovery can impair judgment and increase errors.' | 'building in intentional pauses'; 'batch non-urgent updates, protect focus windows'; 'protecting time for check-ins, shared reflection, and dialogue.' HBR (via Willison blockquotes): 'AI introduced a new rhythm in which workers managed several active threads at once'; 'While this sense of having a "partner" enabled a feeling of momentum, the reality was a continual switching of attention'. Quote wording from the fetch tool's extraction; re-check against the page before printing [uncertain].
date_and_recency: Published 9 Feb 2026 (HBR); interview 18 Feb 2026. Data collection: eight months, April to December 2025 per Willison summary.
key_claims: AI tools did not reduce work in the studied firm; employees worked faster, took on broader task scope and extended work into more hours, largely without being asked. Workers ran several threads at once (manual work while AI generates, parallel agents, reviving deferred tasks), producing constant task switching, frequent checking of AI outputs and a growing list of open tasks. Expectations reset so extra effort becomes standard. Authors propose an 'AI practice': intentional pauses, sequencing/batching, protected focus windows, and human check-ins and reflection.
headline_figures: About 200 employees at one US-based technology company; eight-month study (April to December 2025); more than 40 semi-structured interviews (Ye, Haas interview). The '62% report unsustainable workloads' figure on a forum post is NOT from this study as far as verified; exclude. Twice-weekly observation claim is from a forum only [uncertain].
sample_unit_and_population: One anonymised US technology company, around 200 employees across functional groups (not specifically software engineers; engineers were among those described coding with AI). Company did not mandate AI but offered enterprise subscriptions to commercial tools.
observed_vs_stated: Mixed ethnography. Observed: Ye on site regularly watching work in real time, plus tracking of communication channels (the latter from a forum post only [uncertain]). Self-reported: 40+ semi-structured interviews on workflows, time and end-of-day feelings (busier, more stretched, less able to disconnect). The load and fatigue claims lean on self-report; the extended hours and task-scope claims rest on observation and interviews together, not on time logs.
what_makes_oversight_tiring: Per Willison's quote of HBR and the Haas interview: managing several active threads, continual attention switching, frequent checking of AI outputs, a growing backlog of open tasks, and reduced recovery time. Ye: constant switching and reduced recovery can impair judgment.
consequence_for_quality: Ye: constant switching and reduced recovery 'can impair judgment and increase errors'. Secondary coverage says HBR reports cognitive fatigue, burnout and weakened decision-making [uncertain: HBR body not opened]. No measured error rates reported in anything I opened.
what_reduces_the_load: An 'AI practice' of norms: intentional pauses before major decisions, batching non-urgent updates, protecting focus windows, and protected time for check-ins, shared reflection and dialogue. Recommendations are the authors' proposals, not tested interventions.
limitations_stated: Described as in-progress research with initial findings, one company. No explicit limitations list found in the opened material (single-firm limit is the fetch tool's inference).
counter_evidence: Not searched in depth. Single firm, non-peer-reviewed, no control group or objective time data seen; worker enthusiasm and voluntary uptake means intensification may be self-chosen rather than imposed.
verification_status: Checked against opened source (Haas newsroom interview): method, 40+ interviews, workload creep quotes, norms. Checked via second-hand quotation only: HBR 'several active threads' and 'continual switching' lines. NOT checked against HBR body: burnout and 'weakened decision-making' wording, 'unsustainable', exact eight-month window of April to December 2025 [uncertain]. HBR page paywalled.
usable_claim: In an in-progress, eight-month study of about 200 employees at one US tech company, Ranganathan and Ye observed and interviewed staff and reported that AI use led people to work faster, take on more, and work longer hours, with several concurrent threads and constant checking of AI output adding cognitive load. Their proposed remedy is team norms such as pauses and protected focus time.
do_not_use: The '62% unsustainable' figure; claims of measured burnout rates or error rates; generalisation to software engineers or all firms; any quote from the HBR body not seen directly; 'twice-weekly observation' and '40 interviews' as HBR facts without the Haas citation.
overlap_with_existing_essays: Not checked against the trust essay, Verification Gap or Checking Isn't Catching in this run [uncertain].
